# FTP Footprinting

> Essential FTP fundamentals, Linux server configuration with vsFTPd, and practical footprinting and enumeration techniques.

- **Author:** [Ahmed Ibrahim Asl (ASL)](https://eng-asl.com/about/)
- **Canonical URL:** https://eng-asl.com/notes/security/footprinting/ftp/
- **Markdown URL:** https://eng-asl.com/notes/security/footprinting/ftp.md
- **Category:** Security / Footprinting
- **Published:** 2026-11-27
- **Updated:** 2026-11-27
- **Ports:** TCP 21 (Control), TCP 20 / PASV (Data)
- **Daemon:** vsFTPd (/etc/vsftpd.conf)
- **Tags:** Security, Footprinting, FTP, vsFTPd, Linux, Enumeration

## How FTP Works

FTP (File Transfer Protocol) is an application-layer protocol in the TCP/IP stack (alongside HTTP and POP) used to transfer files between a client and a server over TCP.

Unlike single-connection protocols, FTP separates commands and file transfers across two distinct TCP connections.

| Channel | Purpose | Port |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Control Channel | Commands and server responses. | TCP 21 by default. |
| Data Channel | Files and directory listings. | TCP 20 as the traditional Active mode source port (depending on configuration), or a negotiated server port in Passive mode. |

#### Diagram: FTP Dual TCP Channels

FTP separates commands on TCP port 21 from file transfers and directory listings on a dedicated Data Connection.

Illustration URL: https://eng-asl.com/media/notes/security/footprinting/ftp/ftp-two-channels.png

Diagram description: Diagram distinguishing Client and FTP Server connected by Control Channel on TCP port 21 (commands USER, PASS, LIST, STOR, RETR, PORT, PASV and status codes) and a separate Data Channel for file transfers and listings.

- Control Channel stays on TCP port 21 for commands (USER, PASS, LIST, STOR, RETR, PORT, PASV) and numeric status codes.
- Data Channel opens a second TCP socket for file payloads and directory listings.
- Both channels carry traffic bidirectionally once established.

### Control Channel

The Control Channel exchanges FTP commands and server responses. It normally remains open throughout the FTP session.

#### Inspect Control Channel

Persistent TCP control session (default port 21) used to negotiate authentication, data modes, file commands, and status responses.

- TCP connection establishment: Client initiates a three-way handshake to server TCP port 21 before any FTP commands are sent.
- Client and server communication: Both ends send ASCII protocol commands and numeric replies bidirectionally over this control stream.
- USER and PASS authentication: Credentials (or anonymous login) are submitted on the control socket unless TLS via AUTH TLS protects the stream.
- PORT and PASV negotiation: Coordinates which IP and TCP port will carry the next Data Channel transfer.
- LIST, RETR, and STOR commands: Trigger directory listings, file downloads, and file uploads.
- Three-digit response codes: Server status codes such as 220, 230, 200, 150, 226, and 530 synchronize every step.
- Session lifecycle and termination: Stays open across multiple transfers until the client sends QUIT (221 Goodbye) or the server idle timeout expires.

### Data Channel

The Data Channel transfers files and directory listings. It is normally opened when a transfer is required and closed when that transfer finishes.

#### Inspect Data Channel

On-demand TCP connection dedicated to transferring directory listings and file payloads cleanly alongside the Control Channel.

- Temporary TCP connections: Opened for a single LIST, RETR, or STOR transfer and closed cleanly once complete.
- Uploading and downloading: Carries file bytes from client to server on STOR and from server to client on RETR.
- Directory listings: Returns folder entries and permissions on LIST or LIST -R rather than mixing raw file listings into control replies.
- Transfer lifecycle and Control relationship: Negotiated on the Control Channel first (200 after PORT/PASV, 150 before opening, 226 upon closing).
- Port negotiation: Uses client-advertised ports in Active mode or server-advertised ephemeral ports in Passive mode.
- Transfer restart markers: Interrupted transfers can resume when both client and server support restart markers (REST).
- Initiation vs transfer direction: Whichever host initiates the TCP socket (server in Active mode, client in Passive mode) does not restrict which direction file bytes flow afterward.

## Active and Passive FTP

FTP supports two modes for establishing the Data Connection. In both modes, the client initiates the Control Connection.

| Mode | Connection initiator |
| --- | --- |
| Active FTP | Server |
| Passive FTP | Client |

### Active FTP

The client uses the `PORT` command to tell the server which client endpoint to connect to. The server initiates the Data Connection back to that endpoint.

#### Explore Active FTP

Mode in which the client advertises a listening endpoint with PORT and the server initiates the Data Connection back.

1. Client port 51000 connects to server port 21 to open the Control Connection.
2. Client sends PORT on the control channel to advertise its listening data endpoint, for example port 51001.
3. Server initiates the Data Connection toward client port 51001, traditionally from source port 20 when configured (such as connect_from_port_20=YES).
4. File data or directory listings then travel in the required direction.

##### Diagram: Active FTP (PORT)

Client connects from port 51000 to server port 21, sends PORT 51001, and the server initiates the Data Connection back (traditionally from source port 20).

Illustration URL: https://eng-asl.com/media/notes/security/footprinting/ftp/ftp-active-mode.png

Diagram description: Active FTP sequence showing client port 51000 opening control socket to server port 21, advertising client port 51001 via PORT, and server port 20 initiating the Data Connection back to client port 51001.

- Client initiates Control Connection to server TCP port 21.
- Client sends PORT specifying its listening endpoint (e.g. port 51001).
- Server initiates the Data Connection back toward client port 51001.

**Security Note:** Client-side firewalls and NAT routers commonly block incoming TCP connections initiated by the remote server toward client port 51001.

### Passive FTP

The client uses the `PASV` command to request a server listening endpoint. The client then initiates the Data Connection outbound.

#### Explore Passive FTP

Mode in which the server opens a listening port after PASV so the client initiates both Control and Data Connections outbound.

1. Client port 51000 connects to server port 21 to open the Control Connection.
2. Client sends PASV over the control channel.
3. Server replies with an ephemeral listening data port, for example port 52000.
4. Client connects outbound from a local ephemeral port (for example 51002) to server port 52000.

##### Diagram: Passive FTP (PASV)

Client connects to server port 21, sends PASV, receives a server listening port (e.g. 52000), and opens both TCP connections outbound.

Illustration URL: https://eng-asl.com/media/notes/security/footprinting/ftp/ftp-passive-mode.png

Diagram description: Passive FTP sequence showing client port 51000 connecting to server port 21, sending PASV, receiving listening port 52000, and client port 51002 initiating the Data Connection outbound to server port 52000.

- Client initiates Control Connection to server TCP port 21.
- Server replies to PASV with its listening ephemeral data port (e.g. port 52000).
- Client connects outbound from a local ephemeral port (e.g. 51002) to server port 52000.

**Security Note:** Passive FTP generally traverses client-side firewalls and NAT more reliably because all connections originate outbound from the client, though the server must allow inbound traffic to its configured passive data port range.

#### Diagram: Complete FTP Overview Visual Sheet

Illustration URL: https://eng-asl.com/media/notes/security/footprinting/ftp/ftp-overview-full.jpg

Combined visual summary of FTP Dual TCP Connections (Control TCP 21 and Data Channel), Active FTP (PORT), Passive FTP (PASV), authentication, cleartext transport, and anonymous access.

## vsFTPd

vsFTPd (Very Secure FTP Daemon) is a commonly used Linux FTP server. FTP defines the communication protocol, while vsFTPd implements it on the host.

A daemon is a program that provides a background service. The default configuration file is `/etc/vsftpd.conf`.

#### vsFTPd Setup Guide

Install the vsFTPd package, filter active directives from /etc/vsftpd.conf, and consult the manual for omitted defaults.

- Package installation runs on Debian or Ubuntu via apt and places default configuration in /etc/vsftpd.conf.
- Note on filtering: grep -v "#" excludes every line containing a hash character (#) anywhere on the line, including settings followed by an inline # comment, rather than only full-line comments.
- /etc/vsftpd.conf omits many supported options; run man vsftpd.conf to inspect every directive and default behavior.

##### Diagram: FTP Protocol and Daemon Capabilities

Visual reference contrasting FTP capabilities, password authentication, plain-text transport exposure, and anonymous access.

Illustration URL: https://eng-asl.com/media/notes/security/footprinting/ftp/ftp-quick-facts.png

Diagram description: Visual summary strip covering FTP operations, username/password login, cleartext security exposure, and anonymous FTP.

- FTP defines the protocol; software such as vsFTPd implements it on the server.
- Standard FTP transmits credentials and payloads in plain text.

**1. Install vsFTPd**

```bash
$ sudo apt install vsftpd
```

**2. View lines without # in /etc/vsftpd.conf**

```bash
$ cat /etc/vsftpd.conf | grep -v "#"
```

**3. Open full configuration manual**

```bash
$ man vsftpd.conf
```

## vsFTPd Configuration Settings

Directives in `/etc/vsftpd.conf` govern network listeners, authentication, filesystem isolation, listings, banners, logging, and TLS.

### Network and Connection Settings

| Setting | Description |
|---|---|
| `listen=NO` | Controls standalone IPv4 operation. When YES, vsFTPd listens independently. When both listen and listen_ipv6 are NO, a superserver such as inetd can start vsFTPd when a connection is requested. |
| `listen_ipv6=YES` | Enables independent listening on an IPv6 socket, which may also accept IPv4 connections depending on system configuration. |
| `connect_from_port_20=YES` | Configures vsFTPd to use server TCP port 20 as the source port for Active FTP Data Connections. |

On-demand operation saves memory when FTP is rarely used. It does not hide the FTP service from port scanning because another service such as `inetd` still listens on port 21.

#### Service Startup & On-Demand Operation

Standalone listening vs superserver activation (listen, listen_ipv6, and connect_from_port_20).

- Standalone IPv4 (listen=YES): vsFTPd remains running in the background listening on IPv4 TCP port 21.
- On-demand mode (both listen=NO and listen_ipv6=NO): Another service such as inetd holds TCP port 21 and launches vsFTPd only when needed, saving RAM when FTP is rarely used.
- Default Linux distributions often set listen=NO alongside listen_ipv6=YES so one dual-stack IPv6 socket handles connections independently.
- Active FTP source port (connect_from_port_20=YES): Requests outgoing Active Data Connections originate from port 20, though Active data port behavior remains configuration-dependent.

**Security Note:** On-demand startup does not conceal FTP from Nmap or port scanners because inetd or systemd still keeps TCP port 21 open and listening.

### Authentication and Access Control

| Setting | Description |
|---|---|
| `anonymous_enable=NO` | Disables anonymous login. |
| `local_enable=YES` | Allows existing Linux system accounts to authenticate to FTP. |
| `pam_service_name=vsftpd` | Selects the PAM authentication configuration, normally at /etc/pam.d/vsftpd. PAM is also used by SSH and sudo. |
| `secure_chroot_dir=/var/run/vsftpd/empty` | Defines an empty, restricted directory used to isolate pre-authentication vsFTPd processes from system files. |

Before authentication, the process handling incoming FTP commands does not require direct access to sensitive system files. vsFTPd isolates this process inside `secure_chroot_dir` under the Principle of Least Privilege; this is not the directory used for sharing, uploading, or downloading files.

#### Pre-Auth Process Isolation (secure_chroot_dir)

Confines unprivileged pre-authentication vsFTPd command handlers inside empty directory /var/run/vsftpd/empty.

- Principle of Least Privilege: Pre-login command handlers parse network input without needing visibility into /etc, /home, or /var.
- Distinct purpose: secure_chroot_dir=/var/run/vsftpd/empty is reserved exclusively for daemon isolation and is never used for user file sharing, uploads, or downloads.

##### Diagram: Pre-Login Sandbox Isolation (secure_chroot_dir)

Unprivileged pre-authentication vsFTPd command handlers run inside empty directory /var/run/vsftpd/empty, separated from /etc, /home, and /var.

Diagram description: Diagram showing incoming FTP commands routed into an isolated vsFTPd process confined inside /var/run/vsftpd/empty, isolated from /etc, /home, and /var.

- Applies the Principle of Least Privilege to unauthenticated control handlers.
- Not used for sharing, uploading, or downloading user files.

**Security Note:** Chroot limits filesystem traversal to a restricted directory tree; it is not a complete security boundary that prevents every possible form of process or kernel compromise.

### Ownership and User Restrictions

| Setting | Description |
|---|---|
| `chown_uploads=YES` | Changes the ownership of anonymously uploaded files. |
| `chown_username=username` | Specifies the Linux account receiving ownership. |
| `chroot_local_user=YES` | Restricts local FTP users to their configured root directory. |
| `chroot_list_enable=YES` | Enables `/etc/vsftpd.chroot_list`, whose behavior depends on `chroot_local_user`. |

Authenticated user confinement applies to `/etc/vsftpd.chroot_list`, which is distinct from pre-login `secure_chroot_dir` isolation.

#### Authenticated User Chroot Rules

Controls whether authenticated local Linux accounts can browse outside their home directories via chroot_local_user and /etc/vsftpd.chroot_list.

- Process isolation vs user restriction: secure_chroot_dir isolates pre-auth vsFTPd workers inside an empty directory, whereas chroot_local_user restricts authenticated local logins after authentication.
- Enabling write permissions on a chrooted home directory interacts with vsFTPd writeable-chroot protections (allow_writeable_chroot).

**Behavior when chroot_list_enable=YES (/etc/vsftpd.chroot_list)**

| chroot_local_user | Users in the enabled chroot list |
| --- | --- |
| YES | Exceptions to the restriction (can browse outside their home). |
| NO | Users who are restricted (everyone else remains unrestricted). |

**Security Note:** Accidental reversal of YES/NO leaves system directories readable to FTP logins. As with all chroot configurations, treat chroot as defense-in-depth filesystem restriction rather than an absolute sandbox.

### Information Disclosure and Directory Listing

| Setting | Description |
|---|---|
| `hide_ids=YES` | Displays file owners and groups as ftp instead of real UIDs or usernames. |
| `ls_recurse_enable=YES` | Enables recursive directory listings using LIST -R. |

Enabling `hide_ids` alters displayed ownership fields in FTP protocol listings without changing actual file ownership or Linux permissions.

#### Compare Directory Listings (hide_ids & Fail2ban)

*Source: Illustrative example*

Contrasts raw UID/username disclosure in FTP listings against masked ftp/ftp ownership with hide_ids=YES.

- hide_ids=YES rewrites displayed owner and group strings to ftp in protocol LIST output without changing real Linux UID/GID ownership or on-disk permissions.
- Exposed usernames (or UID numbers tied to shared host accounts) help attackers assemble valid username lists for brute-force or credential-stuffing attacks against FTP or SSH.
- Defensive layer: Properly configured Fail2ban monitors authentication logs (such as vsFTPd or SSH failures) and bans offending client IPs after repeated failed login attempts.

**FTP listing comparison** *(Illustrative example)*

```text
-rw-rw-r-- 1 1002 1002 Calendar.pptx   # Default listing exposes UID/owner
-rw-rw-r-- 1 ftp  ftp  Calendar.pptx   # With hide_ids=YES enabled
```

### Messages, Time and Logging

| Setting | Description |
|---|---|
| `dirmessage_enable=YES` | Displays a message when a user enters a configured directory. |
| `message_file=.message` | Defines the file containing the directory entry notice. |
| `ftpd_banner=Welcome to FTP Server` | Defines the 220 welcome greeting directly inside vsftpd.conf. |
| `banner_file=/etc/ftp_banner.txt` | Loads the welcome greeting from a file and overrides ftpd_banner. |
| `use_localtime=YES` | Displays directory timestamps using server local time rather than GMT. |
| `xferlog_enable=YES` | Logs file uploads and downloads for auditing. |

### Encryption and Security

| Setting | Description |
|---|---|
| `ssl_enable=NO` | Disables TLS support. Set to YES to allow FTPS connections. |
| `rsa_cert_file` | Path to the server X.509 TLS certificate. |
| `rsa_private_key_file` | Path to the private key paired with the certificate. |

Standard FTP transfers credentials and file contents in plain text. Enabling TLS support (`ssl_enable=YES`) and enforcing encrypted logins or data transfers are separate configuration concerns.

| Protocol | Security |
| --- | --- |
| FTP | Plain text. |
| FTPS | FTP with TLS encryption. |
| SFTP | File transfers over SSH using a separate protocol. |

#### Transport Security: FTP, FTPS, and SFTP

Separates cleartext FTP from TLS-encrypted FTPS (rsa_cert_file, rsa_private_key_file, ssl_enable) and SSH-based SFTP.

- Default Debian/Ubuntu certificate paths commonly point to /etc/ssl/certs/ssl-cert-snakeoil.pem (rsa_cert_file) and /etc/ssl/private/ssl-cert-snakeoil.key (rsa_private_key_file).
- Enabling TLS vs enforcing TLS: Setting ssl_enable=YES enables FTPS capability on vsFTPd, whereas enforcing encryption for all sessions requires additional directives such as force_local_logins_ssl and force_local_data_ssl.
- FTP and SFTP are separate protocols: FTPS wraps RFC 959 FTP over TLS inside vsFTPd, while SFTP is the SSH File Transfer Protocol subsystem running over SSH.

##### Diagram: FTP vs FTPS vs SFTP Transport Security

Contrasts unencrypted plain-text FTP, TLS-wrapped FTPS, and SSH-tunneled SFTP.

Diagram description: Diagram contrasting plain-text FTP, SSL/TLS-encrypted FTPS, and SSH-based SFTP.

- Standard FTP sends credentials and payloads in plain text.
- FTPS wraps FTP control/data sockets in TLS.
- SFTP operates over SSH and is a distinct protocol from FTP.

**Security Note:** Standard plain-text FTP exposes usernames, passwords, commands, and file payloads to passive packet capture on shared networks.

## FTP Users and Access Control

The `/etc/ftpusers` file lists usernames that are denied FTP access when the authentication policy enforces this denylist.

**Inspect /etc/ftpusers**

```bash
$ cat /etc/ftpusers
```

Enforcing this list helps prevent sensitive or privileged Linux accounts from authenticating over FTP unnecessarily.

#### PAM Authentication and /etc/ftpusers Denylist

*Source: Illustrative example*

How /etc/pam.d/vsftpd enforces the /etc/ftpusers denylist to block privileged or designated accounts.

- When PAM rules in /etc/pam.d/vsftpd invoke pam_listfile.so (pointing to /etc/ftpusers), listed accounts receive 530 Login incorrect even with valid OS passwords.
- Administrators add root, service accounts, or restricted local usernames to reduce attack surface.
- Note: Example entries such as guest, john, and kevin illustrate file structure only and are not universal Linux defaults; real defaults typically block system accounts such as root, daemon, and nobody.

**Illustrative /etc/ftpusers entries** *(Illustrative example)*

```bash
$ cat /etc/ftpusers
guest
john
kevin
```

## Dangerous Settings and Anonymous Access

Anonymous FTP permits access without a personal user account. It can support internal distribution, yet permissive settings risk exposing files or allowing unauthorized writes.

| Setting | Description |
|---|---|
| `anonymous_enable=YES` | Allows anonymous login. |
| `no_anon_password=YES` | Removes the anonymous password prompt. |
| `anon_root=/home/username/ftp` | Sets the directory exposed as root to anonymous users. |
| `write_enable=YES` | Enables filesystem-modifying FTP commands. |
| `anon_upload_enable=YES` | Allows anonymous uploads when required permissions permit. |
| `anon_mkdir_write_enable=YES` | Allows anonymous directory creation when permitted. |

Anonymous access risks include unauthorized reads, filename disclosure, and unintended file uploads or disk consumption; anonymous writes require both `write_enable=YES` and matching Linux filesystem write permissions.

#### Anonymous Access Risk Scenarios

Operational and security consequences of permissive anonymous_enable, no_anon_password, anon_root, and write flags.

- Information disclosure: Public directory trees and leftover backup or template files under anon_root reveal internal projects, client names, or credentials.
- Unauthorized uploads: write_enable=YES plus anon_upload_enable=YES (with writable Linux permissions) allows external clients to upload malware, Phishing assets, or unwanted payloads.
- Unauthorized file modification or deletion: Existing files in shared upload paths can be overwritten or removed via STOR and DELE.
- Storage abuse: Repeated uploads or directory creation via anon_mkdir_write_enable=YES can exhaust server disk quotas and disrupt local services.

**Security Note:** Keep anon_root non-writable for anonymous FTP accounts unless an isolated, non-executable dropbox is explicitly required.

## Anonymous Login and Server Enumeration

Connecting to port 21 reveals the server welcome banner, authentication policy, and exposed directory listings. Use `anonymous` in authorized tests (lab host `10.129.14.136`).

**Connect and list directory**

```text
$ ftp 10.129.14.136
Name: anonymous
ftp> ls
```

Folder and file names often reveal internal workflows or account hints even when downloading individual files is restricted.

#### Complete Anonymous FTP Login and ls Output

*Source: Abbreviated output*

Anonymous connection on 10.129.14.136 showing the 220 banner, 230 login reply, passive/active hints, and root directory listing.

- 220 welcome greeting discloses server software (vsFTPd) or organization context.
- 230 confirms unauthenticated anonymous login succeeded; 150 and 226 wrap the directory Data Connection.

##### Diagram: Anonymous Login and Enumeration Flow

Protocol sequence from receiving banner code 220 through anonymous login (230) and directory listing (150 to 226).

Diagram description: Sequence diagram illustrating TCP 21 connection, 220 welcome banner, anonymous login 230, and ls listing 150 to 226.

- 220 carries server greeting and software hints.
- 230 confirms anonymous login succeeded; 150 and 226 bracket Data Channel transfers.

**Anonymous FTP session** *(Abbreviated output)*

```text
$ ftp 10.129.14.136
Connected to 10.129.14.136.
220 "Welcome to the HTB Academy vsFTP service."
Name: anonymous
230 Login successful.
Remote system type is UNIX.
Using binary mode to transfer files.
ftp> ls
200 PORT command successful. Consider using PASV.
150 Here comes the directory listing.
Calender.pptx
Clients/
Documents/
Employees/
Important Notes.txt
226 Directory send OK.
```

### Common FTP Response Codes

| Code | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `220` | Service ready. |
| `230` | Login successful. |
| `200` | Command successful. |
| `150` | About to open the Data Connection. |
| `226` | Data transfer completed. |
| `530` | User not logged in. |

## Debugging FTP Communication

FTP clients provide diagnostic commands to inspect local client settings and raw protocol exchanges.

| Command | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| status | Displays local FTP client settings. |
| quote STAT | Requests status information from the FTP server. |
| debug | Displays FTP protocol commands issued by the client. |
| trace | Enables packet tracing when supported by the client. |

The `status` command inspects the local client, whereas `quote STAT` sends a protocol query to the remote server.

#### Debug, Trace, Status, and quote STAT Output

*Source: Abbreviated output*

Complete client status flags, server-returned 211 STAT report, and outgoing PORT/LIST commands with debug and trace active.

- Client visibility caveat: debug and trace increase client-side protocol visibility; they do not force the FTP server to disclose extra data beyond what STAT or normal replies already emit.
- ---> prefixes outgoing client commands sent over the TCP 21 Control Channel.

##### Diagram: Local Client Diagnostics vs Server STAT

Separates client-side inspection commands (status, debug, trace) from server-queried session details (quote STAT).

Diagram description: Diagram separating local FTP client visibility commands (status, debug, trace) from server query command (quote STAT).

- status, debug, and trace inspect client configuration and outgoing commands locally.
- quote STAT sends an FTP protocol STAT command to query remote server state.

**Client diagnostics and server STAT exchange** *(Abbreviated output)*

```text
ftp> status
Connected to 10.129.14.136.
No proxy connection.
Mode: stream; Type: binary; Form: non-print; Structure: file
Verbose: on
Debugging: off
Use of PORT cmds: on
ftp> quote STAT
---> STAT
211 FTP server status:
     Connected to 10.10.14.4
     Logged in as ftp
     TYPE: ASCII
     No session bandwidth limit
     Session timeout in seconds is 300
     Control connection is plain text
     Data connections will be plain text
     At session startup, client count was 1
     vsFTPd 3.0.3 - secure, fast, stable
211 End of status
ftp> debug
Debugging on (debug=1).
ftp> trace
Packet tracing on.
ftp> ls
---> PORT 10,10,14,4,188,195
200 PORT command successful. Consider using PASV.
---> LIST
150 Here comes the directory listing.
226 Directory send OK.
```

## Recursive Directory Listing

When `ls_recurse_enable=YES` is active on the server, the client can enumerate accessible subdirectories recursively.

**Recursive directory listing**

```text
ftp> ls -R
```

This maps nested accessible folders without changing directories manually.

#### Recursive Directory Structure (ls -R)

*Source: Reconstructed directory tree*

Nested hierarchy mapped when ls_recurse_enable=YES allows LIST -R across client workspaces, templates, and notes.

- Distinction from raw LIST -R: Raw FTP servers emit sequential directory stanzas ending in 226 Directory send OK; the tree layout below reconstructs that nested hierarchy for clarity.

**FTP Root hierarchy** *(Reconstructed directory tree)*

```text
ftp> ls -R
FTP Root
├── Calendar.pptx
├── Clients
│   ├── HackTheBox
│   │   ├── appointments.xlsx
│   │   ├── contract.docx
│   │   ├── contract.pdf
│   │   └── meetings.txt
│   └── Inlanefreight
│       ├── appointments.xlsx
│       ├── contract.docx
│       ├── meetings.txt
│       └── proposal.pptx
├── Documents
│   ├── appointments-template.xlsx
│   ├── contract-template.docx
│   └── contract-template.pdf
├── Employees
└── Important Notes.txt
```

## Downloading and Uploading Files

Authorized verification tests read access (`get`, `wget`) and write access (`put` / `STOR`) within agreed scope boundaries.

### Download a File

Use `get` (escaping spaces in filenames) to download a single file from the server.

**Download single file**

```text
ftp> get Important\ Notes.txt
```

#### Single File Download Output (get)

*Source: Abbreviated output*

Binary transfer sequence retrieving Important Notes.txt over the Data Connection.

- Code 150 opens the binary Data Connection and code 226 confirms all 41 bytes were received.

**get transfer log** *(Abbreviated output)*

```text
ftp> get Important\ Notes.txt
150 Opening BINARY mode data connection.
226 Transfer complete.
41 bytes received.
```

### Download Accessible Files

Wget can mirror accessible directories and files in one command.

**Mirror accessible files with Wget**

```bash
$ wget -m --no-passive ftp://anonymous:anonymous@10.129.14.136
```

| Option | Description |
| --- | --- |
| -m | Enables mirroring. |
| --no-passive | Uses Active FTP. |

#### Wget Mirroring Output and Local Directory Tree

*Source: Illustrative example*

Mirroring accessible directories into a local host folder followed by local tree inspection.

- Wget creates a local directory matching the target IP or hostname (10.129.14.136/).

**Wget Active mirror and local tree** *(Illustrative example)*

```bash
$ wget -m --no-passive ftp://anonymous:anonymous@10.129.14.136
Connecting to 10.129.14.136:21... connected.
Logging in as anonymous ... Logged in!
==> SYST ... done.    ==> PWD ... done.
==> TYPE I ... done.  ==> PORT ... done.    ==> LIST ... done.
...
Downloaded: 15 files
$ tree 10.129.14.136
10.129.14.136
├── Calendar.pptx
├── Clients
│   ├── HackTheBox
│   └── Inlanefreight
├── Documents
└── Important Notes.txt
```

**Security Note:** Bulk downloads generate noticeable network traffic and server log entries that trigger intrusion monitoring; perform mirroring strictly inside authorized scopes.

### Upload a File

The `put` command sends a local file using FTP `STOR`; completion confirms write permissions on the destination directory.

**Test write permission safely**

```text
$ touch testupload.txt
ftp> put testupload.txt
```

#### File Upload Output (put / STOR)

*Source: Abbreviated output*

Client put session translating to FTP STOR to verify write access safely with an empty file.

- Use a harmless empty marker file when testing write access rather than uploading active payloads during initial footprinting.

**STOR upload session** *(Abbreviated output)*

```text
ftp> put testupload.txt
---> STOR testupload.txt
150 Ok to send data.
226 Transfer complete.
```

### Security Implications

Writable FTP directories become critical when shared with downstream services such as web application roots. Upload permission alone does not grant code execution; additional vulnerabilities, loose permissions, or insecure integrations are required.

#### Conditional Security Implications of Writable FTP

How writable FTP folders intersect with downstream services, and the preconditions required for severe impact.

- Unauthorized file modification: Replacing static templates, scripts, or shared documents.
- Information exposure: Writing configuration traps or reading shared internal resources.
- Local File Inclusion (LFI): If a vulnerable web application includes files located inside the writable FTP folder.
- FTP log poisoning: If server transfer or error logs containing user-controlled filenames/strings are parsed unsafely or included by a web script.
- Remote Code Execution (RCE) and privilege escalation: Conditional outcomes when an executable script lands inside a web root, cron job, or privileged import path.

**Security Note:** Important qualification: FTP upload access alone does not execute files. Code execution occurs only when chained with secondary weaknesses, excessive OS permissions, or insecure web/application integrations.

## Footprinting FTP with Nmap

Nmap detects FTP services, versions, and configuration exposure using the Nmap Scripting Engine (NSE).

### FTP Scripts

NSE scripts are commonly stored under `/usr/share/nmap/scripts/`. Running `--script-updatedb` rebuilds Nmap's local script database index rather than downloading new scripts.

**Rebuild script index and locate FTP scripts**

```bash
$ sudo nmap --script-updatedb
$ find / -type f -name "ftp*" 2>/dev/null | grep scripts
```

#### FTP Nmap Scripting Engine (NSE) Reference

Installed FTP scripts in /usr/share/nmap/scripts/ cover discovery, configuration checks, brute-forcing, and specific vulnerability probes.

- Remember: Having an installed vulnerability-checking NSE script does not imply the scanned target is vulnerable.
- Always check NSE script categories and raw responses before acting on script findings (https://nmap.org/book/nse.html).

**Common FTP NSE scripts**

| Script | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| ftp-anon | Checks whether anonymous FTP login is allowed and lists root entries. |
| ftp-syst | Sends SYST and STAT queries to gather server software and status. |
| ftp-bounce | Tests whether PORT allows bouncing connections to third-party hosts. |
| ftp-brute | Performs dictionary authentication audits in authorized scopes. |
| ftp-vsftpd-backdoor | Checks for the historic vsFTPd 2.3.4 backdoor. |
| ftp-proftpd-backdoor | Checks for a known ProFTPD source-tampering backdoor. |
| ftp-vuln-cve2010-4221 | Probes ProFTPD for CVE-2010-4221 stack buffer overflow. |
| ftp-libopie | Checks FTP daemons linked against vulnerable libopie versions. |

### Service Enumeration

Run a focused FTP version and default-script scan:

**Focused FTP scan**

```bash
$ sudo nmap -sV -sC -p21 10.129.14.136
```

| Option | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| -sV | Service and version detection. |
| -sC | Default NSE script scanning. |
| -p21 | Scans TCP port 21. |

Output can reveal anonymous access, server software versions, accessible directories, and session parameters.

#### Full Nmap FTP Enumeration Output

*Source: Abbreviated output*

Complete port 21 service enumeration result including ftp-anon anonymous listing and ftp-syst server configuration details.

- Original source scan command: sudo nmap -sV -p21 -sC -A 10.129.14.136.
- Flag redundancy note: Because -A already enables version detection (-sV) and default NSE scripts (-sC), passing -sV and -sC alongside -A is redundant; -sV -sC -p21 suffices when OS fingerprinting and traceroute are not needed.

**Original source scan example** *(Abbreviated output)*

```bash
$ sudo nmap -sV -p21 -sC -A 10.129.14.136
PORT   STATE SERVICE VERSION
21/tcp open  ftp     vsftpd 2.0.8 or later
| ftp-anon: Anonymous FTP login allowed (FTP code 230)
|_-rw-r--r--   1 ftp      ftp          41 Jul 20  2022 Important Notes.txt
| ftp-syst:
|   STAT:
| FTP server status:
|      Connected to 10.10.14.4
|      Logged in as ftp
|      TYPE: ASCII
|      No session bandwidth limit
|      Session timeout in seconds is 300
|      Control connection is plain text
|      Data connections will be plain text
|      At session startup, client count was 3
|      vsFTPd 3.0.3 - secure, fast, stable
|_End of status
Service Info: OS: Unix
```

### Nmap Script Trace

Adding `--script-trace` logs network exchanges sent and received by NSE scripts.

**Trace NSE packet exchanges**

```bash
$ sudo nmap -sV -sC -p21 10.129.14.136 --script-trace
```

#### Nmap --script-trace NSOCK Communication Log

*Source: Abbreviated output*

Shows raw NSE socket connections, client ephemeral source ports, control commands, and server responses.

- Local ephemeral vs target ports: 10.10.14.4:54228 and 10.10.14.4:54230 are client-side ephemeral source ports allocated locally by the scanner OS, whereas 10.129.14.136:21 is the fixed listening FTP service port.
- Each NSE script may establish an independent TCP control session using a distinct local source port.

##### Diagram: Nmap Script Trace Ephemeral Source Ports

NSE scripts open distinct local ephemeral source ports (such as 54228 and 54230) toward target FTP port 21.

Diagram description: Client-server trace diagram showing scanner 10.10.14.4 using ephemeral local ports 54228 and 54230 to query target 10.129.14.136 port 21.

- Different NSE scripts establish independent TCP sockets from local ephemeral ports.
- Target listening port remains TCP port 21.

**NSOCK trace excerpt** *(Abbreviated output)*

```bash
$ sudo nmap -sV -sC -p21 10.129.14.136 --script-trace
NSE: TCP 10.10.14.4:54228 > 10.129.14.136:21 | CONNECT
NSE: TCP 10.10.14.4:54228 < 10.129.14.136:21 | 220 Welcome to HTB-Academy FTP service.
NSE: TCP 10.10.14.4:54228 > 10.129.14.136:21 | USER anonymous
NSE: TCP 10.10.14.4:54228 < 10.129.14.136:21 | 230 Login successful.
NSE: TCP 10.10.14.4:54228 > 10.129.14.136:21 | PASV
NSE: TCP 10.10.14.4:54228 > 10.129.14.136:21 | LIST
NSE: TCP 10.10.14.4:54228 > 10.129.14.136:21 | CLOSE
NSE: TCP 10.10.14.4:54230 > 10.129.14.136:21 | CONNECT
NSE: TCP 10.10.14.4:54230 < 10.129.14.136:21 | 220 Welcome to HTB-Academy FTP service.
NSE: TCP 10.10.14.4:54230 > 10.129.14.136:21 | USER anonymous
NSE: TCP 10.10.14.4:54230 > 10.129.14.136:21 | SYST
NSE: TCP 10.10.14.4:54230 < 10.129.14.136:21 | 215 UNIX Type: L8
NSE: TCP 10.10.14.4:54230 > 10.129.14.136:21 | STAT
```

## Manual FTP Interaction and TLS

Netcat and Telnet probe banners and raw commands on TCP port 21, while OpenSSL inspects FTPS certificates over STARTTLS.

### Manual Interaction

Netcat and Telnet open raw control connections on port 21 for manual commands, though they do not automatically manage separate FTP Data Connections.

**Connect with Netcat or Telnet**

```bash
$ nc -nv 10.129.14.136 21
$ telnet 10.129.14.136 21
```

#### Manual Netcat / Telnet FTP Interaction

*Source: Illustrative example*

Raw TCP port 21 banner capture and manual USER/PASS control interaction without an FTP client.

- Netcat and Telnet speak only to the single TCP Control Connection and do not spawn or bind secondary FTP Data Connections automatically.

**Manual nc control exchange** *(Illustrative example)*

```bash
$ nc -nv 10.129.14.136 21
Connection to 10.129.14.136 21 port [tcp/ftp] succeeded!
220 Welcome to HTB-Academy FTP service.
> USER anonymous
331 Please specify the password.
> PASS anonymous
230 Login successful.
> QUIT
221 Goodbye.
```

### FTP over TLS

OpenSSL upgrades a plain-text FTP control socket via `-starttls ftp` to inspect TLS parameters and X.509 certificates. Certificate Subject fields may reveal hostnames or organization names, but should not be trusted as verified identity, especially for self-signed certificates.

**Inspect FTPS certificate with OpenSSL**

```bash
$ openssl s_client -connect 10.129.14.136:21 -starttls ftp
```

#### OpenSSL STARTTLS Certificate and Chain

*Source: Abbreviated output*

Full FTPS certificate fields, verification message, certificate chain, and negotiated TLS 1.3 cipher details retrieved via -starttls ftp.

- OpenSSL opens TCP 21 as plain FTP, sends AUTH TLS, and upgrades to TLS before reading the server certificate.

**Extracted Certificate Metadata**

| Field | Example Value |
| --- | --- |
| Country | US |
| State | California |
| Locality | Sacramento |
| Organization | Inlanefreight |
| Organizational Unit | Dev |
| Common Name | master.inlanefreight.htb |
| Email Address | admin@inlanefreight.htb |
| Certificate Type | Self-signed (verify error:num=18) |

**OpenSSL s_client -starttls ftp session** *(Abbreviated output)*

```bash
$ openssl s_client -connect 10.129.14.136:21 -starttls ftp
CONNECTED(00000003)
depth=0 C = US, ST = California, L = Sacramento, O = Inlanefreight, OU = Dev, CN = master.inlanefreight.htb, emailAddress = admin@inlanefreight.htb
verify error:num=18:self-signed certificate
verify return:1
---
Certificate chain
 0 s:C = US, ST = California, L = Sacramento, O = Inlanefreight, OU = Dev, CN = master.inlanefreight.htb, emailAddress = admin@inlanefreight.htb
   i:C = US, ST = California, L = Sacramento, O = Inlanefreight, OU = Dev, CN = master.inlanefreight.htb, emailAddress = admin@inlanefreight.htb
---
Server certificate
-----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----
... (PEM certificate omitted for brevity) ...
-----END CERTIFICATE-----
---
SSL-Session:
    Protocol  : TLSv1.3
    Cipher    : TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384
    Verify return code: 18 (self-signed certificate)
---
220 Welcome to HTB-Academy FTP service.
```

**Security Note:** Self-signed X.509 certificate Subject fields can contain arbitrary values and must not be assumed authentic without independent verification.

# Engineering Field Notes: Methods and Tests

> How I document embedded systems, Linux, cybersecurity, Flutter, and AI work so another engineer can reproduce the result.

- **Author:** [Ahmed Ibrahim Asl (ASL)](https://eng-asl.com/about/)
- **Canonical URL:** https://eng-asl.com/notes/welcome-to-field-notes/
- **Markdown URL:** https://eng-asl.com/notes/welcome-to-field-notes.md
- **Category:** Notes
- **Published:** 2026-07-20
- **Updated:** 2026-07-25
- **Difficulty:** All levels
- **Tags:** Engineering, Linux, Documentation

A project page shows the finished system. These field notes record the decisions
behind it: commands, measurements, failed approaches, and checks that proved the
result.

## Topics I cover

The archive focuses on work I can test and explain:

- embedded systems, firmware, sensors, and connected-device architecture;
- Linux, networking, and legal cybersecurity challenges;
- Flutter interfaces for physical products;
- robotics and control systems;
- AI and machine-learning experiments with reproducible inputs and results.

Some entries are short references. Longer walkthroughs include the environment,
commands, expected output, failure modes, and files needed to repeat the work.

## How I write a walkthrough

A walkthrough should help the reader recognize the problem again. My longer
articles follow a consistent structure:

1. define the goal and constraints;
2. record the environment and prerequisites;
3. show the investigation or design process;
4. explain the working solution;
5. document common failure modes;
6. finish with reusable checks or lessons.

> A useful technical note gives the reader a method they can apply elsewhere.

## Reproducible examples

Commands appear in copyable terminal blocks:

```bash
ssh user@example-host -p 2220
```

I record versions, dependencies, configuration, and expected output when they
change the result. Security articles stay within legal labs, owned systems, and
defensive learning.

## Series in progress

The OverTheWire Bandit walkthrough covers Linux commands and problem-solving in
a controlled challenge environment. The Learn With Me series develops practical
foundations in Linux, Python, Dart and Flutter, and Git.

The archive grows alongside active engineering and teaching work. If an entry
helps another person verify a result or avoid a repeated mistake, it has served
its purpose.
